verified_metadata.title: Input Convex Neural Networks
verified_metadata.venue: Proceedings of the 34th International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 70:146–155

metadata_sources.supports: Official proceedings metadata: exact title, ordered authors, ICML 2017, volume 70 and pages 146–155.

artifact.version_note: Official ICML/PMLR paper; title, authors and proceedings line read and matched.

contexts.evidence: Section 3.1, Proposition 1 gives non-negative hidden weights and non-decreasing activations; with all weights constrained, coordinatewise monotonicity follows.
Section 3 introduces sign-constrained input-convex architectures. Its main motivation is convex inference; interpretability is the thesis’s synthesis.
Section 3.1, equation (2), Proposition 1: non-negative hidden-to-hidden weights and convex non-decreasing activations ensure input convexity.
Section 3.1 allows unrestricted input-to-hidden matrices; these passthrough terms depend affinely on the input.
Proposition 1’s proof uses non-negative convex sums and convex non-decreasing composition, exactly the cited composition principle.
Proposition 1 explicitly includes ReLU/max-pooling and the non-negative-sum/composition argument applicable to the stated Maxout streams.
Proposition 1 supplies the convex-composition principle; coordinatewise monotonicity also follows from the stated non-negative maps and maxima.
Section 3.1 supports the feedforward specialization. The unrestricted first affine layer need not be monotone in the original input.
Sections 4–5 study optimization and learning for ICNNs. Using those ideas to accelerate DCINN training is explicitly future work.

notes: The thesis explicitly restricts its ICNN definition to the plain feedforward core; the full paper includes unrestricted affine passthrough connections and partially input-convex architectures. The phrase interpretable core in the introduction is thesis synthesis, not a claim made by Amos et al. No DOI is assigned on the PMLR record.

verified_metadata.title: Shortcomings of Top-Down Randomization-Based Sanity Checks for Evaluations of Deep Neural Network Explanations
verified_metadata.venue: 2023 IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR), pp. 16143–16152

metadata_sources.supports: Official CVF accepted version confirms title, complete ordered authors, CVPR 2023 and page range.
Original preprint identity; key year 2022 refers to preprint, current bibliography correctly cites 2023 publication.

artifact.version_note: Official CVF accepted paper; downloaded and read alongside official supplement Binder2022shortcomings_supplement.pdf.

contexts.evidence: Sections 3–6 distinguish sensitivity under randomization from output faithfulness and caution against ranking explanation quality from similarity alone.
Sections 4–5 explain retained structures/scales; supplement §C proves noise confounds Spearman too. This does not justify exempting HOG/Spearman by omitting SSIM.
contexts.proposed_replacement: We do not report SSIM here. The remaining similarity scores are also complementary diagnostics: \textcite{Binder2022shortcomings} show that input-dependent structure and activation scales can survive top-down randomization, and that low similarity can also reflect noise.

contexts.evidence: Section 6 recommends combining diagnostics rather than using randomization as the sole explanation-quality criterion. Lower similarity measures greater change under this test.

notes: Citation key year 2022 is harmless; published year 2023 is already correct. Unicode page en-dash may be normalized to BibTeX -- as formatting maintenance.

verified_metadata.title: Learning Important Features Through Propagating Activation Differences
verified_metadata.venue: Proceedings of the 34th International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 70:3145–3153

metadata_sources.supports: Official proceedings title, complete ordered authors, ICML 2017, volume 70 and pages.

artifact.version_note: Official ICML/PMLR publication; title/authors and methods §§3.1, 3.5.2 read.

contexts.evidence: Section 3 defines DeepLIFT using reference differences, summation-to-delta and backward multipliers, supporting its inclusion among principled attribution methods.
Sections 3.1 and 3.5.2 explicitly permit nonzero DeepLIFT contributions when local gradients vanish. Thus information loss does not affect every backward-pass method as asserted.
contexts.proposed_replacement: This section identifies a structural information loss affecting methods that propagate ordinary local derivatives through the original graph at the evaluated input, and shows how the split-pair representation of Section~\ref{sec:dc_splitting_relu} preserves separate stream signals.

contexts.evidence: Section 3.5.2 defines Rescale multipliers as finite activation differences relative to reference activations; the CNN-only restriction describes the thesis experiment.

notes: DeepLIFT is organized around reference differences and summation-to-delta; the broad axiomatic-family label should not imply that it satisfies every Integrated Gradients axiom. Nearby saliency.tex:17 repeats the every-attribution-method overstatement; restrict that statement consistently even though it is outside this entry’s supplied citation paragraphs.

contexts.evidence: §7.2, p. 233 models both positive excitatory and negative inhibitory weights. Page 239 explains Dale's law as a common sign for a neuron's outgoing connections and explicitly retains excitatory and inhibitory populations. It does not support the stronger equation of exclusively additive networks with biologically plausible processing.
contexts.proposed_replacement: Networks with non-negative weights implement a computation in which every neuron can only \emph{add} evidence, never cancel it --- a scheme long associated with interpretability~\parencite{ayinde2018nonnegativity,lee1999nmf}.

notes: The publisher page lists author identities in a different order; the actual title page and author website establish Peter Dayan followed by L. F. Abbott, so the existing order should be retained. Initials L. F. are the book's printed author form; expansion to Laurence F. in verified_metadata comes from the publisher.
